record.paper_title: Models, feedback control, and open problems of 3D bipedal robotic walking
record.original_question: Construct a metric for comparing walking gaits, including a distance between solutions of hybrid systems even when the underlying hybrid models are different, so that one can decide which controller and which hybrid model produce the most human-like walking. Such a metric should also support comparison between robotic walking data and human walking data.

evidence.quote: A question is: which controller for which hybrid model yields the most human-like walking Miura et al. [2011]?

In order to answer this question, a metric on the distance between walking gaits is needed, i.e., a metric for comparing the distance between solutions of hybrid systems even in the case when the hybrid models are different.
This could then be used to both compare different controllers—through a comparison of the resulting periodic solutions—and to compare robotic walking with human walking

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. A hybrid dynamical system is a tuple H = (Γ, D, U, S, Δ, F) consisting of a directed graph Γ with vertices V and edges E, a domain D_v ⊂ R^{n_v} and admissible control set U_v for each v ∈ V, a guard (switching surface) S_e ⊂ D_{source(e)} and a reset map Δ_e : S_e → D_{target(e)} for each e ∈ E, and a family of controlled vector fields F_v on D_v. An execution (solution) of H is a piecewise-smooth trajectory that flows under F_v inside each domain and jumps across edges via Δ_e whenever it reaches a guard. A periodic walking gait of a bipedal robot or a human is a periodic execution of such a hybrid system.

Two different bipedal walkers (e.g., a robot model with given mechanical parameters and feedback controller, or a human modeled from motion-capture data) are typically described by hybrid systems H_1 and H_2 whose graphs, domain dimensions, guards, and reset maps need not coincide.

Problem. Construct a metric d that assigns to any pair (x_1, x_2) of executions of (possibly distinct) hybrid systems H_1 and H_2 a nonnegative real number d(x_1, x_2) such that:

(i) d is a metric (nonnegativity, identity of indiscernibles up to a natural equivalence, symmetry, and triangle inequality) on a space containing executions of arbitrary hybrid systems of the above form, including the case H_1 ≠ H_2 with differing graphs, domain dimensions, guards, and reset maps;

(ii) d restricts to a meaningful distance on periodic gaits, so that, given a fixed hybrid robot model H with various feedback controllers producing periodic solutions x^*_1, …, x^*_k, the value d(x^*_i, x^*_human) ranks the controllers by closeness to a reference human gait x^*_human (which is itself an execution of a different hybrid system H_human);

(iii) d is computable from finite measured trajectory data and is well-defined when applied to recorded robotic walking data and recorded human walking data.

Provide an explicit construction of such a metric, prove that it satisfies the metric axioms, and demonstrate that it can distinguish "more human-like" from "less human-like" gaits in a principled way.
artifact.status_search_result: No general metric on solutions of hybrid systems with differing underlying models has been established in the literature. Existing approaches (e.g., RMSE on spatiotemporal/kinematic features, the Combined Gait Asymmetry Metric CGAM, and various task-specific gait similarity scores) compare gaits via fixed scalar parameter sets rather than as solutions of hybrid dynamical systems with possibly different graphs, dimensions, guards, and resets. The general problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Comparing Gait with Multiple Physical Asymmetries Using Consolidated Metrics (CGAM)
status_evidence.snippet: CGAM is designed to combine spatial, temporal, kinematic, and kinetic gait parameter asymmetries into a single number quantifying gait.
status_evidence.claim: Existing gait comparison metrics operate on fixed parameter sets, not on solutions of differing hybrid systems.

status_evidence.title: Simulation of human gait with body weight support: benchmarking models and unloading strategies
status_evidence.snippet: RMSE with respect to human data is used to compare the accuracy of gait models on spatiotemporal parameters and vertical ground reaction forces.
status_evidence.claim: State of the art still uses ad-hoc RMSE on selected features rather than a true metric on hybrid system executions.
